title: Applying stages, exception and products to a scenario
blurb: Separate manage by stages, manage by exception and focus on products in a scenario, and judge how well each is applied.
question: At the end of a stage, a project board approves the next stage plan and sets a time tolerance of two weeks for it. Is setting that tolerance manage by stages or manage by exception, and why?

teach.body: Manage by stages, manage by exception and focus on products all appear in planning and control, so examiners use them as near misses for each other. Separate them by what the action decides. WHEN the board next makes a decision is stages. HOW FAR a plan may vary before someone escalates is exception. WHAT will be delivered, and to what quality, is products.

teach.caption: The 'near miss' row shows actions that sound like the column's principle but belong to another.

teach.body: Formally: the project is planned, monitored and controlled stage by stage, with at least two stages, the first being initiation. In plain English: the board gets review and decision points, and the project is properly initiated before delivery starts. Authority is delegated one stage at a time. Shorter stages give more control; longer ones ease the burden on senior managers. Stage ends can be timed to show the effect of an external influence, such as a budget cycle.

teach.h: Brennan Mutual's stages and decision points (S6)
teach.caption: Each stage end is a decision point. The pilot wave of ten low-risk applications sits in its own stage before the main waves.

teach.body: Formally: limits of delegated authority are set by defining tolerances for the seven aspects of performance (benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability, risk), and a FORECAST breach is escalated to the next level. In plain English: inside the limits, get on with it; if you expect to go outside them, say so early. Senior managers save time without losing control, and decisions are made at the right level.

teach.h: Tolerances flow down, exceptions flow up

steps.label: Team manager
steps.sub: Works within them; raises forecast breaches

teach.caption: A forecast breach goes up one level at a time: team manager to project manager, project manager to board, board to business layer.

teach.body: Formally: the project focuses on defining and delivering products, especially their quality expectations and requirements. In plain English: be output-oriented, not work-oriented, and do no more work than the agreed products need, which keeps scope creep out. Product descriptions give clarity: purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality criteria and quality method, and who reviews and approves. They drive planning, quality and change control.

children.label: Manage by stages
children.sub: Stage ends, stage length, initiate first

teach.h: Worked scenario: Brennan Mutual, Project Skyline (S6)
items: Five stages, with a pilot wave of ten low-risk applications before the main waves, give the board decision points before most of the risk is taken on: manage by stages.
The chief operating officer proposes a cost tolerance of plus or minus 7.5% and wants to know at once if a wave is FORECAST to slip by more than two weeks: manage by exception.
Every migrated application must pass performance and resilience tests, have operating procedures and a tested rollback: quality criteria in product descriptions, so focus on products.
The chief information officer wants a new data platform added. It is not one of the agreed products, so it goes through change control rather than being started quietly: focus on products.

teach.text: Setting tolerances for the next stage happens AT a stage boundary but applies MANAGE BY EXCEPTION. Likewise, defining what is in scope is focus on products, while the permitted range around it (scope tolerance) is manage by exception. And an exception is a FORECAST breach: waiting until the tolerance has actually been exceeded applies the principle poorly.

items: Stages (2.4): decision points, initiation first, one stage at a time, stage length matched to control needed.
Exception (2.5): tolerances on seven aspects, escalate a forecast breach early, within tolerance the manager decides.
Products (2.6): output not work, product descriptions with quality criteria, no more work than the agreed products need.
Ask what the action settles: when, how far, or what.

summary: You can now separate manage by stages, manage by exception and focus on products in a scenario by asking whether an action settles when, how far or what. You can also judge an application as good or poor using the reason that fits the facts.

A.q: Carrowford City Council's half marathon will cut its riverside festival if entries are below 6,000 by the end of June. The project manager proposes that stage 2 should end in the last week of June, so the board sees the final entry figure before it authorizes the build-up stage. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Manage by stages, because shorter stages give the project board more control over the work
Manage by stages, because a stage end can be timed to show the effect of an outside influence
Manage by exception, because the council's net contribution has been capped at £300,000
Focus on products, because the festival elements are products whose scope may be reduced
A.why: Manage by stages lets stage ends be aligned with external influences, such as a budget-setting cycle, so their impact is clear at the decision point (2.4). Here the influence is the entry total.

whyNot.0: Shorter stages do give more control, but the stage is not being shortened; its end is being placed at a meaningful date.
whyNot.2: The cap is a real limit, but the action is about when the board decides, not about tolerances.
whyNot.3: The festival scope may change later, but the action is about the timing of the decision point.

A.q: On Brennan Mutual's data centre exit, the project manager's forecast shows that a delay in wave 2 will take the stage three weeks past its planned end, against a stage time tolerance of two weeks, although nothing has yet slipped. She sends an exception report to the board that day instead of waiting for the next monthly highlight report. How well does this apply the 'manage by exception' principle, and why?
options: It applies it well, because the board must approve every change to the stage plan
It applies it well, because the next level should hear as early as possible of a forecast breach
It applies it poorly, because a breach should be reported once tolerance has actually been exceeded
It applies it poorly, because the project manager should first use the change budget to recover
A.why: The point of manage by exception is to alert the next management level as early as possible when work is forecast to move outside tolerance (2.5). A forecast breach is enough.

whyNot.0: Within tolerance the project manager adjusts the plan without the board; only a forecast breach needs the board.
whyNot.2: An exception is a forecast breach; waiting for the actual breach loses the time the board needs to respond.
whyNot.3: A change budget pays for approved changes, not for recovering a forecast delay beyond tolerance.

A.q: On Fernhollow Foods' ready meal launch, the project manager agrees a description for each recipe before development starts. Each one sets an eight-day minimum shelf life, the supermarket's technical standard, allergen controls, a carbon limit of 1.5 kg CO2e per meal and who will approve the recipe. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Focus on products, because the project should do no more work than its agreed products need
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because each description names the approver
Manage by exception, because quality tolerance comes from the recipe quality specifications
Focus on products, because product descriptions give a shared view of each product and its quality
A.why: Focus on products uses product descriptions to give clarity about each product's purpose, composition and quality criteria, including who approves it (2.6).

whyNot.0: Avoiding extra work is part of 2.6, but this action defines quality up front; it does not cut out work.
whyNot.1: Naming the approver is one line of a product description, but the action is defining the products.
whyNot.2: Quality tolerance does come from specifications, but the action is writing the specifications, not setting a range.

B.q: At Tarnside College the project board meets at the end of stage 3. It approves the stage 4 plan and, in the same meeting, sets a cost tolerance of plus or minus 2% and a time tolerance of two weeks for stage 4. Which principle is being applied by setting these tolerances, and why?
options: Manage by stages, because the board authorizes the next stage at the stage boundary
Manage by exception, because tolerances set the limits of authority delegated to the PM
Manage by stages, because authority is delegated to the project manager a stage at a time
Manage by exception, because decisions should be taken at the most local level possible
B.why: Defining tolerances establishes the limits of delegated authority, which is manage by exception (2.5), even though it happens at a stage boundary.

whyNot.0: Authorizing the next stage is manage by stages, but the question asks about setting the tolerances.
whyNot.2: Delegating a stage at a time is part of 2.4, but the action here is fixing the size of the limits, which is exception.
whyNot.3: Local decision-making is how exception applies to people (3.5.1), but the stem is about the board setting stage tolerances.

B.q: On Brennan Mutual's data centre exit, the chief information officer asks for a new data platform to be built as part of the project. The project manager points out that it is not one of the products in the agreed project product description and asks for it to be raised as a request for change. How well does this apply the 'focus on products' principle, and why?
options: It applies it poorly, because the data platform would add benefits to the business case
It applies it poorly, because a senior manager's request should be built into the plan
It applies it well, because scope tolerance lets the project manager decide on small additions
It applies it well, because the project should do no more work than its agreed products need
B.why: Focus on products means the project does no more work than it needs to deliver its agreed products, which controls scope creep (2.6). A new product must go through change control.

whyNot.0: Possible extra benefits are assessed when the request for change is considered; they do not justify starting work outside the agreed products.
whyNot.1: Seniority does not change the scope; the request needs assessing and deciding by the right authority.
whyNot.2: A whole new platform is not a small variation, and scope tolerance belongs to manage by exception in any case.

B.q: At Wenmoor Community Health, the planned final stage covers evaluation of the pilot and roll-out to two localities over 24 weeks. Because the rural locality has strong GP resistance, the board asks for the roll-out to be split into two stages, one per locality, so it can decide again before the second roll-out. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Manage by stages, because shorter stages give more control where the work carries more risk
Manage by stages, because every project starts with an initiation stage before delivery
Learn from experience, because an earlier central booking attempt in the rural area failed
Manage by exception, because tolerances let the board limit what the PM decides in each area
B.why: Stage length is a trade-off: shorter stages give more control, longer stages reduce the burden on senior managers (2.4). Higher risk justifies an extra decision point.

whyNot.1: Initiation always comes first, but that fact does not explain splitting a later stage.
whyNot.2: The earlier failure may inform the risk, but the action is adding a decision point, which is stages.
whyNot.3: Tolerances limit authority, but the board is creating a new decision point, not setting limits.

C.q: At Wenmoor Community Health, initiation is in its fourth week. The head of nursing for the pilot locality says her team is overstretched and asks for the new triage hub to open now. The executive agrees, and the hub starts taking referrals before the project initiation documentation is approved. Is this an appropriate application of the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because the pilot locality was already planned to have the triage hub first
Yes, because the PM can adjust the work while the stage is forecast within tolerance
No, because the commissioner must approve the pilot before it is allowed to start
No, because the project should be properly initiated before delivery work begins
C.why: Manage by stages ensures the project is properly initiated before work starts on delivering its outputs (2.4). Opening the hub during initiation skips that decision point.

whyNot.0: The pilot was planned for a later stage; the plan does not authorize delivery before initiation is complete.
whyNot.1: Adjusting work within tolerance is allowed, but starting delivery during initiation is not an adjustment; it bypasses the board's decision.
whyNot.2: Nothing in the method requires the commissioner's approval; the issue is that the board has not authorized the project.

C.q: On Calderbrook's permit project the stage time tolerance is two weeks. The project manager forecasts that the discovery and alpha stage will finish three days late, so she sends an exception report to the board and asks for direction. Is this an appropriate application of the 'manage by exception' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because the board should be alerted early about any slippage in the stage
Yes, because the fixed live date makes every delay a matter for the board
No, because the forecast is within tolerance, so the PM should handle it
No, because exception reports are sent to the business layer, not the board
C.why: Within tolerance the project manager has authority to act; escalating a forecast that stays within tolerance wastes senior management time (2.5). The delay belongs in the next highlight report.

whyNot.0: Early warning applies to a forecast BREACH of tolerance; three days inside a two-week tolerance is not an exception.
whyNot.1: The live date matters, but the board has already set the tolerance it is willing to accept for this stage.
whyNot.3: A stage-level exception report goes from the project manager to the project board.

C.q: On Carrowford's half marathon, the build-up stage plan lists activities such as 'hold meetings', 'phone volunteers' and 'chase suppliers', but there is no product description for the event safety plan that the safety advisory group must approve. The project manager says the team knows what a safety plan is. Is this an appropriate application of the 'focus on products' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because an experienced team can tailor away formal planning documents
Yes, because activity lists are needed to estimate the time and cost of the work
No, because the safety plan needs a description setting its quality criteria and approver
No, because the safety plan belongs in the project plan rather than the stage plan
C.why: Focus on products is output-oriented: the safety plan is a key product, so its product description should set its purpose, composition, quality criteria and who reviews and approves it (2.6).

whyNot.0: Tailoring adjusts how the method is used; it cannot remove a principle, and this team has never run an event of this scale.
whyNot.1: Activities are needed for estimates, but a work-oriented plan without product definitions is the opposite of this principle.
whyNot.3: A product delivered in this stage belongs in the stage plan; the problem is the missing product description.

reteach.title: When, how far, what
reteach.question: If you had to label the action with one word, would it be 'when', 'how far' or 'what'?

blocks.body: WHEN: the board's next decision point, the length of a stage, finishing initiation first. That is manage by stages. HOW FAR: the tolerance on cost, time, scope or another aspect, and raising a forecast breach early. That is manage by exception. WHAT: the products, their descriptions, their quality criteria, and not doing work beyond them. That is focus on products.

head: Stem says
Principle
rows: Board wants to see the PID before delivery starts
Stage end timed to a budget or entry deadline
Tolerance set for the next stage
PM raises a forecast breach early
Extra product refused without change control

blocks.text: Where the action happens is not what it applies. A tolerance set at a stage boundary is still exception; a product description agreed at a stage boundary is still products.

explain.body: Initiation is always the first stage. The board sees the project initiation documentation and authorizes the project before any delivery work starts. That gate is manage by stages.

test.q: On Brennan Mutual's data centre exit, the chief operating officer, as executive, asks the project manager to present the completed project initiation documentation to the board before any work on the cloud landing zone begins. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Manage by exception, because senior managers save time while keeping control
Manage by stages, because the project is properly initiated before delivery starts
Manage by exception, because the next level must be alerted early to forecast problems
Manage by stages, because the PM may adjust work while the stage stays in tolerance
test.why: Managing by stages ensures the project is properly initiated before work starts on delivering its outputs (2.4). The landing zone is delivery work.

whyNot.0: Saving senior managers' time is a purpose of exception, but the request is for a decision point before delivery.
whyNot.2: Early alerts concern forecast breaches of tolerance; nothing here is forecast to breach.
whyNot.3: That is part of 2.4, but it does not explain why the PID must be presented before delivery.

explain.body: Each level delegates to the next by setting tolerances: business layer to board (project), board to project manager (stage), project manager to team manager (work package). Inside the limits, the lower level decides.

test.q: On Calderbrook's permit project, the project manager gives the supplier's delivery manager a work package for the payment pages with a time tolerance of three days and a cost tolerance of £5,000, within the stage tolerances set by the board. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Manage by stages, because the work package fits inside the current stage plan
Focus on products, because the work package describes the products to be built
Manage by exception, because authority is delegated to the next level by tolerances
Manage by exception, because the board should hear at once about any package delay
test.why: Accountability is established by delegating authority from one level to the next with tolerances (2.5). The work package tolerances set the team manager's limits.

whyNot.0: The package does sit in the stage plan, but the action asked about is setting its tolerances.
whyNot.1: A work package does reference product descriptions, but the stem is about the limits of authority.
whyNot.3: Delays inside work package tolerance are handled by the team manager; only forecast breaches go up, and to the project manager first.

explain.body: An exception exists as soon as a tolerance is FORECAST to be exceeded. Raising it then gives the next level time to act. Waiting for the actual breach is the poor application examiners look for.

test.q: At Fernhollow Foods, the line supplier warns that delivery of the new tray-sealing line will be three weeks late. The project manager's forecast shows this would push the stage beyond its two-week time tolerance, although no deadline has been missed yet. She raises an exception report at once. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Manage by exception, because a forecast breach of tolerance is escalated to the next level
Manage by stages, because the board must authorize any new plan for the rest of the stage
Manage by exception, because decisions belong at the most local level with the knowledge
Ensure continued business justification, because a late line could threaten the launch week
test.why: Manage by exception escalates to the next level when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded (2.5), as early as possible.

whyNot.1: The board may later approve an exception plan, but the action is raising the exception, which is manage by exception.
whyNot.2: Local decision-making is how exception applies to people, but here the decision is beyond the project manager's tolerance.
whyNot.3: The launch risk matters to the business case, but the action is escalating a forecast breach.

explain.h: Describe the product, not the work
explain.body: A product description states purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality criteria and quality method, and who reviews and approves. It lets everyone agree what 'done' means before work starts.

test.q: At Tarnside College the project manager writes a description of the welding bay area before design work starts, setting its purpose, the 24 bays with fume extraction, the extraction standard to be met, and the lead welding instructor as a reviewer. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: Focus on products, because a product description sets what the product is and its quality
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because a reviewer is named for the area
Manage by exception, because the extraction standard sets the quality tolerance for the area
Focus on products, because the project should do no more work than its products need
test.why: Focus on products uses product descriptions to define each product's purpose, composition, quality criteria and who reviews it (2.6).

whyNot.1: Naming a reviewer is one part of the description; the action as a whole defines the product.
whyNot.2: Quality tolerance is drawn from specifications, but writing the specification is product definition.
whyNot.3: Avoiding extra work is part of 2.6, but nothing here is being cut; the product is being defined.
